reference_answer: Self-RAG trains the LM to emit special reflection tokens. A retrieval token, predicted from the input and preceding generation, decides whether retrieving passages would help and calls the retriever on demand. Critique tokens then judge the relevance of each retrieved passage and whether the generated output is supported and useful, and are used to pick the best continuation.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: CRAG's lightweight retrieval evaluator scores how relevant the retrieved documents are and maps the score to one of three actions: Correct, Incorrect or Ambiguous. When the action is Incorrect, CRAG discards the retrieved documents and turns to large-scale web search for external knowledge instead; for Correct it refines the documents into knowledge strips, and Ambiguous combines both.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RAPTOR splits text into chunks, embeds them with SBERT as leaf nodes, clusters similar chunks, and uses a language model to summarise each cluster. The summaries are re-embedded and the embed-cluster-summarise cycle repeats until further clustering is infeasible, giving a bottom-up multi-layer tree whose parent nodes summarise their children. At query time it retrieves from different levels of the tree.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Accuracy follows a U-shaped curve: models use relevant information best when it is at the beginning (primacy) or end (recency) of the context and perform worst when it is in the middle. For example, GPT-3.5-Turbo's multi-document QA accuracy can drop by more than 20%, in the worst case below its closed-book accuracy (56.1%).
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) first instructs an instruction-following LLM such as InstructGPT to write a hypothetical document answering the query. An unsupervised contrastively trained encoder (Contriever) embeds that document, and its vector is used to retrieve similar real documents. The hypothetical document captures relevance patterns even if it contains false details, so no relevance labels are needed.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: GraphRAG uses an LLM to build a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the corpus, partitions the graph into a hierarchy of communities of closely related entities, and pre-generates a summary for each community. For a global question, community summaries each produce partial answers in parallel, which are then aggregated (map-reduce) into a final global answer, which vector RAG cannot do over a whole corpus.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RAGAS is a reference-free framework that scores RAG pipelines with prompted LLM metrics for faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance. ARES instead fine-tunes lightweight LLM judges on synthetic data and uses a small human-annotated set with prediction-powered inference to give confidence intervals. ARES's paper reports that it ranks RAG systems more accurately than RAGAS, with Kendall's tau 0.065 higher for context relevance and 0.132 higher for answer relevance.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: IRCoT interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought: after each reasoning sentence it generates, it uses that sentence as a new query to retrieve more passages, so retrieval happens at every CoT step. FLARE retrieves actively and only when needed: it generates a temporary next sentence and, if it contains low-probability tokens, uses it as a query to retrieve documents and regenerate the sentence; if the model is confident it keeps the sentence without retrieving.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: DPR encodes the question and the passage each into a single dense vector with separate BERT encoders and scores them by inner product. ColBERT uses late interaction: it keeps a contextual embedding for every token, encodes query and document independently, and scores with a cheap MaxSim sum over token-level similarities. This keeps document representations pre-computable while capturing finer-grained matching than a single vector.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Several methods decide adaptively whether to retrieve. Adaptive-RAG trains a classifier to predict query complexity and chooses no retrieval, single-step or multi-step retrieval accordingly. Self-RAG predicts a Retrieve reflection token and can trigger retrieval when its probability passes a threshold. FLARE retrieves only when the next generated sentence contains low-confidence tokens.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Methods that interleave retrieval with reasoning for multi-hop QA include IRCoT, which alternates chain-of-thought steps with retrieval and is evaluated on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and IIRC; Iter-RetGen, which iterates retrieval and generation on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue and Bamboogle; and Self-Ask, which asks follow-up sub-questions that can be answered by a search engine.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: HippoRAG 2 keeps HippoRAG's neurobiologically inspired two-stage design (offline indexing into a knowledge graph, online retrieval with Personalized PageRank) but fixes its entity-centric context loss. It integrates passages as well as concepts in the graph, links queries to triples rather than entities, and adds recognition-memory filtering, improving both multi-hop and simple factual QA.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: LightRAG keeps graph-based text indexing but replaces GraphRAG's community-summary pipeline with a dual-level retrieval paradigm that retrieves at both low (specific entity) and high (broader theme) levels, combined with vector search. It is designed to be simpler and faster, supports incremental updates without rebuilding the graph, and reports advantages in comprehensiveness and diversity over GraphRAG and other baselines.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: MultiHop-RAG is a benchmark of multi-hop queries over a knowledge base of news articles, built because earlier RAG benchmarks such as RGB and RECALL mainly test queries answerable from a single piece of evidence.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: DRAGIN decides when to retrieve with RIND (Real-time Information Needs Detection), which considers the LLM's uncertainty about each generated token, the token's influence on later tokens and its semantic significance. It decides what to search for with QFS (Query Formulation based on Self-attention), which builds the query from the tokens the model attends to across the whole context, not only the last sentence.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RAFT builds fine-tuning data where each question comes with a set of documents: 'golden' documents that contain the answer and 'distractor' documents that do not, and a chain-of-thought answer citing the golden document. For part of the data the golden document is left out. Training on this teaches the model to ignore distractors and quote the relevant document in in-domain, open-book RAG.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: ALCE is the first reproducible benchmark for automatically evaluating LLM generations with citations. Systems must retrieve evidence, generate an answer and cite supporting passages, on ASQA, QAMPARI and ELI5. It measures fluency, correctness, and citation quality (citation recall and precision).
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read adds a query rewriting step before retrieval: an LLM (or a small trainable rewriter such as T5-large, trained with reinforcement learning from the reader's feedback) rewrites the input into a search query, a web search engine retrieves with it, and a frozen LLM reader answers. This adapts the query to the frozen retriever and reader.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: For best performance the study recommends a query classification module, 'Hybrid with HyDE' retrieval, monoT5 reranking, 'Reverse' repacking and Recomp summarisation, which gave the highest average score of 0.483 but is computationally intensive. It also gives a balanced recipe that trades a little performance for efficiency.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: The paper proposes two ways. With black-box access, a small NLI model checks whether the retrieved context entails the question-answer and irrelevant context is filtered out. Alternatively, the LLM is fine-tuned on a mix of relevant and irrelevant retrieved contexts so it learns when to use retrieval; about 1,000 examples suffice and make it robust while keeping gains when context is relevant.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Mix-of-Granularity pre-chunks reference documents at several granularity levels and trains a router, inspired by Mix-of-Experts, that selects the best granularity for each query; snippets are then retrieved at the chosen level. The router is trained with soft labels because the ideal granularity is not annotated.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Search-R1 trains the LLM with reinforcement learning (PPO or GRPO) while it interacts with a real search engine during rollouts, masking the loss on retrieved tokens. ZeroSearch avoids real search engines: a lightly fine-tuned LLM simulates the search engine, and a curriculum gradually lowers the quality of the simulated documents, removing API costs and uncontrolled document quality.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RQ-RAG trains the LLM itself on curated data to refine queries explicitly by rewriting, decomposing and disambiguating them, and reports gains on single-hop and multi-hop QA. Rewrite-Retrieve-Read only rewrites the query, using a prompted LLM or a small trainable rewriter (T5-large) in front of a frozen retriever and LLM reader.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RAPTOR organises text into a tree by recursively clustering chunk embeddings and summarising clusters. GraphRAG uses an LLM to extract an entity-relationship knowledge graph, detects communities and pre-summarises them. HippoRAG builds a schemaless knowledge graph of extracted triples as a hippocampus-like index and retrieves with Personalized PageRank from query entities.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: REPLUG treats the language model as a frozen black box and prepends retrieved documents; its LSR variant trains only the retriever using the LM's feedback. RA-DIT fine-tunes both: the LM is instruction-tuned to use retrieved context (LM-ft) and the retriever is tuned to return what the LM prefers (R-ft); combining them gave the largest gain over REPLUG.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Multi-hop dense retrieval (MDR) is a trained dense retriever that retrieves iteratively by concatenating the question with previously retrieved passages to form the next query vector. IRCoT needs no retriever training: it prompts an LLM to generate chain-of-thought and uses each new reasoning sentence as the query for the next retrieval with an off-the-shelf retriever.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Later methods extending adaptive retrieval include DRAGIN, which decides when to retrieve from real-time information needs (token uncertainty, influence and semantics) and forms queries from self-attention, and CtrlA, which detects the need from the model's internal representations (honesty and confidence features) rather than statistical uncertainty. Adaptive-RAG instead chooses a retrieval strategy from predicted query complexity.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: DPR trained a dual encoder with in-batch negatives plus BM25 hard negatives. ANCE draws hard negatives from an approximate-nearest-neighbour index of the model being trained, refreshed asynchronously. RocketQA adds cross-batch negatives, denoised hard negatives (a cross-encoder filters false negatives) and data augmentation.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Graph-based methods that build on GraphRAG's community-based indexing include LightRAG, which uses graph-based text indexing with dual-level retrieval and incremental updates, and ArchRAG, which uses attributed communities from the knowledge graph and a hierarchical index for efficient retrieval.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: DrQA used a fixed TF-IDF document retriever over Wikipedia with a neural reader. ORQA was the first system to learn the retriever and reader jointly end-to-end from question-answer pairs alone, pre-training the retriever with the Inverse Cloze Task. REALM adds retrieval-augmented language model pre-training and backpropagates into the MIPS index, which is refreshed during training.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Not according to the indexed papers; it depends on the setting. One comparison finds that long-context LLMs, when sufficiently resourced, outperform RAG on average, but RAG's much lower cost remains an advantage and a hybrid routes between them. Another finds retrieval helps even long-context models, and that retrieval with a 4K window can match a 16K-context model. The results come from different studies and are not directly comparable.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: No consistent answer. The GraphRAG paper reports that it strongly outperforms vector RAG on global sensemaking questions with GPT-4. Unified evaluations find that graph-based methods do not consistently beat vanilla RAG on every question or on specific QA tasks, and that graph construction adds indexing, latency and storage costs.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: No. Irrelevant or random retrieved contexts can hurt accuracy, and even top-1 Google results hurt on some benchmarks. Lost in the Middle shows that adding more context is a trade-off: performance saturates and the model may miss information in the middle, so more passages do not always help.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: 'Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey' reviews how RAG systems are evaluated: the targets, the datasets and the metrics, including the shift to LLMs as judges.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: 'Modular RAG: Transforming RAG Systems into LEGO-like Reconfigurable Frameworks' proposes a three-tier design of modules, sub-modules and operators, whose orchestration into RAG Flows can express existing RAG methods.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: It re-purposed BERT as a cross-encoder: the query and a candidate passage are fed together into BERT and the [CLS] representation is used to classify relevance. Candidates first retrieved by BM25 are re-ranked by this score. Fine-tuned on the MS MARCO passage ranking dataset, it reached state-of-the-art results on MS MARCO and TREC-CAR.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RECOMP compresses retrieved documents into a short textual summary that is prepended to the input. It uses an extractive compressor, which selects relevant sentences from the retrieved documents, and an abstractive compressor, which generates a summary that synthesises information from several documents. Training uses end-task signals so the compressors can also do selective augmentation, returning little or nothing when the documents do not help.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Chain-of-Note generates sequential reading notes for each retrieved document, assessing how relevant it is to the question, and builds the final answer from these notes. This targets noise robustness (ignoring irrelevant retrieved documents and using intrinsic knowledge) and unknown robustness (answering "unknown" when neither the documents nor the model's knowledge contain the answer).
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Dense X Retrieval proposes propositions as the retrieval unit instead of passages or sentences. A proposition is an atomic expression in the text that captures one distinct factoid in a concise, self-contained natural-language form. The paper finds the choice of retrieval unit significantly affects both retrieval and downstream task performance.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Naive chunking splits the text first and embeds each chunk separately, so chunk embeddings lose context from surrounding text. Late chunking uses a long-context embedding model to run the transformer over all tokens of the long text first, and only then applies chunking, pooling the token representations of each chunk, so every chunk embedding carries information from the whole document.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: LongRAG forms long retrieval units of at least about 4K tokens, using a whole document or grouping related documents (for example Wikipedia pages linked by hyperlinks). A long retriever searches these units and a long-context reader reads the few retrieved units. This shrinks the corpus, gives strong recall with only a few top units, reduces hard negatives and keeps each document's meaning intact.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: A smaller, instruction-tuned specialist RAG drafter generates several answer drafts with rationales, each from a different subset of the retrieved documents. A larger generalist LM then acts as the verifier: it scores the draft-rationale pairs, without re-reading the full retrieved documents, and selects the best answer.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: The paper lists seven failure points: missing content (the answer is not in the documents), missed the top-ranked documents, not in context (the consolidation strategy drops the answer), not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, and incomplete answers. They were derived from three case studies, including one with 15,000 documents and 1,000 questions.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: ColPali encodes document pages directly from their images with a vision-language model (PaliGemma), producing multi-vector embeddings of image patches that live in a space similar to text queries. It matches queries to pages with ColBERT-style late interaction, avoiding the slow layout-detection, OCR and chunking steps of standard indexing.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Fusion-in-Decoder encodes each retrieved passage together with the question independently in the encoder and fuses the evidence only in the decoder, which attends over all encoded passages, so cost grows linearly with the number of passages. RETRO splits the input into chunks, retrieves neighbours for each chunk, encodes them with a retrieval encoder and integrates them through chunked cross-attention layers inside the autoregressive language model.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Query2doc few-shot prompts a large language model to write a pseudo-document for the query and appends it to the query for sparse or dense retrieval. GAR uses a pre-trained language model to generate query contexts (the answer, a sentence containing it, or the title of a relevant passage) and appends them to the query, mainly to improve sparse BM25 retrieval.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: RGB is a benchmark built from recent news that tests four abilities of LLMs in RAG: noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration and counterfactual robustness. RAGChecker is an evaluation framework with claim-level entailment metrics: overall precision, recall and F1 for users, plus modular retriever and generator metrics to diagnose where a RAG system's errors come from.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: HotpotQA was collected from crowd workers who wrote multi-hop questions over Wikipedia and also marked the supporting-fact sentences; it includes comparison questions. MuSiQue is built bottom-up by composing single-hop questions into multi-hop ones under controlled conditions, to reduce reasoning shortcuts and train-test leakage and to add harder distractors, so it is much less solvable by disconnected reasoning.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Izacard and Grave's 'Distilling Knowledge from Reader to Retriever' trains the retriever to approximate the reader's (Fusion-in-Decoder's) cross-attention scores, minimising the KL divergence between retriever scores and normalised attention scores. Atlas adopts this as its Attention Distillation (ADist) loss, using the language model's cross-attention scores as a proxy for each document's importance when training the retriever.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: Fusion-in-Decoder encodes each passage separately and lets the decoder attend over all encoded passages, and most of its time is spent in decoding. FiD-Light compresses each encoded query-passage pair to its first k vectors before the decoder, greatly reducing decoder cost, and adds a source-pointer workflow that re-ranks passages.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: KILT is a benchmark of knowledge-intensive tasks across five task types (such as fact checking, slot filling, question answering and dialogue) aligned to a single Wikipedia snapshot, with provenance annotations so systems can be judged on supporting evidence. Re2G (Retrieve, Rerank, Generate) adds a reranker and end-to-end knowledge distillation and reports state-of-the-art results across five KILT datasets.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: It was written by Scott Barnett, Stefanus Kurniawan, Srikanth Thudumu, Zach Brannelly and Mohamed Abdelrazek, and first posted on arXiv on 11 January 2024 (arXiv 2401.05856).
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review

reference_answer: BEIR includes 18 datasets covering nine different retrieval tasks, ranging from narrow expert domains to open-domain data, for zero-shot evaluation of retrieval models.
source: drafted by Claude (Opus 5.5) from the gold papers' passages; needs team review
